walkthroughs.body_html:
The Living World — a core area of GCSE Geography.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

The Living World brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with The Living World.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between biotic and abiotic components of an ecosystem?
options: Biotic means animals and abiotic means plants.
Tundra is in the Arctic and taiga is in the Antarctic.
Biotic components are all living organisms (plants, animals, microbes); abiotic components are non-living factors (climate, soil, water, light, rock).
Biotic and abiotic both refer to types of soil.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between an ice age and a glacial period?
options: Tundra is in the Arctic and taiga is in the Antarctic.
The ice age ended 10,000 years ago.
Ice ages happen every winter when it gets cold.
An ice age is a long era with permanent ice on Earth (we are still in one); within it, glacial periods (cold) alternate with interglacials (warm) every ~100,000 years driven by Milankovitch cycles.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between the tundra and the taiga biomes?
options: Biotic and abiotic both refer to types of soil.
Tundra is in the Arctic and taiga is in the Antarctic.
Tundra and taiga are the same biome with different names.
Tundra is treeless cold biome (too cold and permafrost-dominated for trees), while taiga (boreal forest) is the band of coniferous forest just south of the tundra in subarctic latitudes.
